title: Natural Language Processing Based Solution for Labeling Brain Metastasis Identified in Radiology Reports
authors: Liu, T.; Han, Y. T.; Zuo, H.; Das, S.; Lin, H.-M.; Colak, E.; Istasy, M.; Ladak, A. M.; Bigenimana, J. C.; Gondara, L.; Simkin, J.; Lee, J.; Roozbeh, D.; Nichol, A. M.; Easaw, J.; Walker, E.; Yip, S.; Mou, L.; Yuan, Y.
abstract: PurposeBrain metastases (BM) far exceed primary CNS tumours and constitute the majority workload for neuro-oncology care providers. Currently, the cancer registries only capture synchronous BMs, which is only a small proportion of all BMs. We aim to develop and validate a natural language processing (NLP) algorithm that identifies brain metastases in radiology reports, enabling scalable surveillance of asynchronous BMs. MethodsUsing population-based cancer registry data in Alberta, Canada, we identified a cancer cohort diagnosed between 2012-2019 with follow-up to 2022. All brain/head radiology reports at and post-cancer diagnosis were identified. Reports were sampled through a multi-phase approach and manually labeled for BM presence. We trained two Bio_ClinicalBERT models on the "Findings" and "Impressions" sections, respectively, and took the maximum predicted probability as the report-level prediction. Internal and external validation used reports from the Canadian provinces of Alberta, Ontario, and British Columbia. ResultsThe models were trained on 1,879 samples. For internal validation, 1,833 reports from 357 patients were tested. At a probability threshold of 0.4, the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.888 and precision of 0.499. The ensemble substantially outperformed single-section models, which achieved sensitivities of only 67.8% (Findings) and 74.2% (Impressions). On external validation, sensitivity was 0.918 in Ontario and 0.726 in British Columbia, demonstrating robustness across diverse data distributions. ConclusionsAn NLP-based pipeline processing both Findings and Impressions sections has been developed and validated in three Canadian provinces. It meets cancer registry operational requirements and to be implemented into the surveillance workflow in Alberta and British Columbia, providing a foundation for population-level BM surveillance.

infographic.key_insight: An NLP ensemble identified brain metastases in radiology reports, supporting cancer surveillance rather than drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The pipeline could help cancer registries capture brain metastases arising after initial cancer diagnosis that current surveillance may miss.
method: Manually labeled brain/head radiology reports from a population-based Alberta cancer cohort.
Trained separate Bio_ClinicalBERT models on Findings and Impressions sections.
Used the higher section-level probability as the report prediction and validated across three Canadian provinces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 1,879 samples, the ensemble achieved 88.8% sensitivity and 49.9% precision on 1,833 internal-validation reports from 357 patients at a 0.4 threshold; external sensitivity was 91.8% in Ontario and 72.6% in British Columbia.
infographic.watch_item: Modest internal precision and variable external sensitivity warrant local validation and review workflows before registry implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Natural Language Processing Based Solution for Labeling Brain Metastasis Identified in Radiology Reports

title: Improving Survival Prediction from Surrogate Endpoints Through Integration of Patient-Reported Outcomes Using Machine Learning
authors: Sun, Y.; Wang, Y.; Luu, H. P. K.; Liu, A.; Zhang, C.; Muluneh, B.; Zheng, W.; Yao, H.; Basch, E.; Zhou, J.
abstract: IntroductionOverall survival (OS) is the gold standard for demonstrating treatment benefit in oncology but requires prolonged follow-up. Surrogate efficacy endpoints, such as progression-free survival, can shorten trial duration and reduce costs but may not consistently reflect overall survival benefit. We hypothesized that integrating patient-reported outcomes (PROs) with surrogate endpoints would improve trial-level prediction of OS benefit. MethodsWe reviewed clinical trials supporting FDA oncology drug approvals from 2013 to 2023 that reported OS, at least one surrogate efficacy endpoint, and PROs. Machine learning models predicted OS benefit were developed using surrogate endpoints alone or surrogate endpoint features combined with PROs. Both models were validated using repeated five-fold trial-grouped cross-validation and leave-one-trial-out validation. ResultsA total of 100 clinical trials (103 between-arm comparisons, 68,987 participants) met inclusion criteria. Compared with control arms, 68% of active treatment arms demonstrated OS benefit, 83.5% showed surrogate endpoints improvement, and 35.9% showed improvement in PROs. Adding PROs to machine learning models increased area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) from 0.67 (95% CI, 0.55-0.78) to 0.79 (95% CI, 0.69-0.87), an absolute increase of 0.12 indicating improved model discrimination. Leave-one-trial-out validation confirmed the improvement (AUC-ROC, 0.663 versus 0.795; paired difference, 0.132; 95% CI, 0.017-0.248). ConclusionsIntegrating PROs with surrogate endpoints improved prediction of OS benefit, supporting machine learning as a quantitative framework for combining complementary endpoints in oncology drug development.

infographic.key_insight: Adding patient-reported outcomes to surrogate endpoints improved machine learning prediction of overall survival benefit in oncology trials.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Combining patient experience with efficacy endpoints could help assess treatment benefit in oncology drug development, without replacing overall survival follow-up.
method: Reviewed FDA approval-supporting oncology trials from 2013–2023 reporting overall survival, surrogate endpoints, and patient-reported outcomes.
Compared machine learning models using surrogate endpoints alone versus surrogate endpoints plus patient-reported outcomes.
Evaluated performance with repeated five-fold trial-grouped cross-validation and leave-one-trial-out validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 100 trials involving 68,987 participants, adding patient-reported outcomes increased AUC-ROC from 0.67 to 0.79; leave-one-trial-out validation supported the improvement (difference 0.132; 95% CI, 0.017–0.248).
infographic.watch_item: Validation was internal to selected approval-supporting trials; generalizability to other trials and individual patient survival prediction remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Survival Prediction from Surrogate Endpoints Through Integration of Patient-Reported Outcomes Using Machine Learning

title: Privacy-Preserving Large Language Model Deployment for Oncology Registry Abstraction: Structure-Aware Evaluation in a Real-World Clinical Setting
authors: Moldovan, M.; Enikeev, R.; Chu, M.; Amalraj, A.; Koli, P. P.; Abdul, S. S.; Sivaraj, H.; Iqbal, U.; Toh, C. K.
abstract: ObjectivesStructuring oncology clinical notes into registry-grade variables is essential for research and care but remains labour-intensive and error-prone. This study developed and evaluated a privacy-preserving large language model pipeline for oncology registry abstraction in a real-world clinical setting. MethodsAn open-source Meta Llama 3.3 70B-based pipeline, prompted without task-specific fine-tuning, was deployed to extract over 50 variables from 6,700 oncology notes at a cancer centre in Singapore. Data were de-identified locally using a Hide-In-Plain-Sight approach, ensuring no identifiable data left hospital infrastructure. Performance was assessed on 200 randomly sampled notes with adjudicated ground truth, using a structure-aware framework that classified outputs as correct, missing, spurious, or incorrect. ResultsF1 scores were high across variables, including diagnosis (97.2%), histology (95.8%), stage (92.6%), biomarkers (91.4%), and treatments (88.1%). Preliminary transferability testing on 50 external notes showed strong performance for core diagnostic variables, with reduced performance for list-valued variables. DiscussionThe structure-aware evaluation approach separated omissions from fabrications, providing more clinically actionable insight than aggregate metrics alone. ConclusionPrivacy-preserving large language models achieved high extraction accuracy under a clinician-verified reference standard, supporting their feasibility for oncology registry abstraction in real-world clinical settings. What is already known on this topicStructuring oncology clinical notes into registry-grade variables is essential for cancer research and care but remains labour-intensive, costly, and inconsistent from one reviewer to the next when performed manually. Large language models offer potential to automate this task, but their use in real-world registries has been limited by concerns over patient data privacy, reliance on task-specific fine-tuning, and evaluation methods that obscure the difference between missing and fabricated information. What this study addsThis study shows that an open-source, privacy-preserving large language model pipeline, deployed entirely within hospital infrastructure without task-specific fine-tuning, can extract over 50 registry variables from oncology notes with high accuracy (F1 scores 88-97% across key variables), validated against ground truth checked by two clinicians. Using a structure-aware evaluation framework, we demonstrate that errors can be meaningfully separated into missing, spurious, and incorrect categories, offering clearer insight into model behaviour than aggregate accuracy metrics alone, and show preliminary evidence of transferability to notes from an external setting. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings support the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, locally hosted large language models for oncology registry abstraction without requiring identifiable data to leave hospital systems or extensive model customisation. The structure-aware evaluation framework is also shared as a reusable template, enabling other institutions to validate similar AI extraction tools in a consistent, clinically meaningful way before wider implementation.

infographic.key_insight: A privacy-preserving Llama 3.3 70B pipeline extracted oncology registry variables with high accuracy without task-specific fine-tuning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support oncology registry abstraction for research and care documentation; it did not evaluate cancer drug discovery or patient outcomes.
method: Extracted over 50 variables from 6,700 oncology notes at a Singapore cancer centre.
Used local Hide-In-Plain-Sight de-identification so identifiable data stayed within hospital infrastructure.
Classified outputs as correct, missing, spurious, or incorrect using structure-aware evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against adjudicated ground truth for 200 randomly sampled notes, F1 scores ranged from 88.1% for treatments to 97.2% for diagnosis; preliminary transferability testing used 50 external notes.
infographic.watch_item: External testing was small and showed reduced performance for list-valued variables, leaving broader generalizability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Privacy-Preserving Large Language Model Deployment for Oncology Registry Abstraction: Structure-Aware Evaluation in a Real-World Clinical Setting

title: Biological age measured by DNA methylation clocks and neurodegenerative diseases: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Kua, Z.; Tay, J. H.; Low, A.; Wang, W.; Yeo, B. T. T.; Dong, Y.; Kandiah, N.; Biessels, G. J.; Maier, A. B.
abstract: Hallmarks of biological ageing are closely interconnected with neurodegenerative diseases. Deoxyribonucleic acid methylation (DNAm) clocks quantify biological age and may serve as peripheral biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to examine associations between DNAm-based biological age metrics and neurodegenerative diseases. Six databases were systematically searched from 1st January 2011 to 15th April 2026 for studies reporting associations between DNAm-based ages and neurodegenerative diseases including all-cause dementia, Parkinsons Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. Correlated-and-hierarchical-effects meta-analyses were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood with Knapp-Hartung adjustment. Of 42,023 records screened, 37 observational studies (n=46 365; 60.5% female; median of mean age 69.4 years [IQR 62.5-73.3)) and seven Mendelian randomization studies met inclusion criteria. In longitudinal meta-analyses, higher GrimAge epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) was significantly associated with higher dementia risk (HR per SD 1.11 [95% CI 1.02-1.20]; I{superscript 2} = 0.0%; p = 0.018), whereas Horvath1 EAA, Hannum EAA, PhenoAge EAA, and DunedinPACE were not significantly associated with dementia risk. Evidence for other neurodegenerative diseases were heterogeneous across clock generations and study designs. Mendelian randomization provided limited evidence for causality. Higher GrimAge EAA was the only DNAm age measure consistently predictive of higher all-cause dementia risk. Overall, however, DNAm age clocks show limited and inconsistent associations with neurodegenerative diseases, providing insufficient support for their use as disease biomarkers. These findings highlight the need to develop and independently validate disease-specific DNAm clocks and undertake pathway analyses to identify methylation changes associated with neurodegeneration and the biological processes they reflect.

infographic.key_insight: GrimAge epigenetic age acceleration was the only DNA methylation age measure consistently associated with higher all-cause dementia risk; overall associations with neurodegenerative diseases were limited and inconsistent.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Current evidence does not sufficiently support DNA methylation clocks as neurodegenerative disease biomarkers.
method: Systematic review across six databases of DNA methylation age measures and neurodegenerative diseases.
Correlated-and-hierarchical-effects meta-analyses with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment.
Included observational and Mendelian randomization studies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review included 37 observational studies involving 46,365 participants and seven Mendelian randomization studies; longitudinal analysis linked GrimAge acceleration to dementia risk (HR per SD 1.11, 95% CI 1.02–1.20).
infographic.watch_item: Causal evidence was limited, and disease-specific clocks require development and independent validation before biomarker use.
infographic.paper_title: Biological age measured by DNA methylation clocks and neurodegenerative diseases: A systematic review and meta-analysis

title: Concussion, Attention, and Mental Health: A Brain Network Study in Youth (CAMBY) - Study Protocol
authors: Scratch, S.; Gill, P. K.; Hickling, A.; Irvin, A.; Zamyadi, R.; Parimoo, S.; Johnston, P. R.; Davis, A. L.; Ibrahim, G. M.; Dunkley, B. T.; Wheeler, A. L.
abstract: BACKGROUNDOne in three adolescents with a concussion history report experiencing long-lasting somatic, sleep, emotional, and/or cognitive disturbances (persisting symptoms after concussion (PSaC)). Cognitive difficulties, such as attentional problems, are common symptoms and can interfere with ongoing development. Clinically, psychiatric symptoms also present in youth with PSaC. A concussion causes diffuse functional and microstructural alterations to neural networks. To develop targeted treatments for PSaC (e.g., neurostimulation), we need to understand how and where structural alterations and neural dysfunction intersect to cause long-lasting symptoms. OBJECTIVES1) Identify functional and microstructural properties in intrinsic connectivity networks, as well as neuropsychological outcomes, that differentiate adolescents with concussion with PSaC from those who do not have PSaC. 2) Determine whether neural activity within intrinsic connectivity networks mediates the relationship between network microstructure and specific neuropsychological features in adolescents with concussion. METHODSCAMBY is a prospective study of adolescents aged 12 to 18 years with a history of concussion. Participants are allocated based on recovery status (PSaC vs. No-PSaC (recovered controls)). Advanced structural (magnetic resonance imaging; MRI) and functional (magnetoencephalography; MEG) neuroimaging and neuropsychological measures will be collected one month or more after concussion. Microstructural and functional features will be computed within intrinsic connectivity networks, then compared between PSaC and recovered control groups and related to symptom domains and neuropsychological profiles. IMPACTThis will be the first study to integrate MRI, MEG, and neuropsychology in adolescents with PSaC to identify disrupted networks underlying PSaC. This observational study is a necessary step towards future clinical trials that accurately target promising therapeutic neurostimulation protocols.

infographic.key_insight: CAMBY will investigate how brain network structure and function relate to persistent attention and mental health symptoms after adolescent concussion—not AI cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Identifying disrupted brain networks could inform future targeted neurostimulation trials for persistent symptoms after concussion.
method: Prospective observational study of adolescents aged 12–18 with a concussion history.
Compare participants with persistent symptoms against recovered concussion controls.
Integrate structural MRI, functional MEG, and neuropsychological assessments collected at least one month after concussion.
infographic.evidence_signal: This protocol plans group comparisons and mediation analyses linking brain network features to neuropsychological outcomes; no study results are reported.
infographic.watch_item: The observational design cannot establish causality or demonstrate that neurostimulation improves symptoms.
infographic.paper_title: Concussion, Attention, and Mental Health: A Brain Network Study in Youth (CAMBY) - Study Protocol
